misconception_description: Student believes that variable names containing vowels can only store string values, while consonant-only names can store any type.

solutions.generated_code:
program CekBilanganPrima
kamus
  nmbr, j, lmt, rmndr : integer
  value : string
  prima : boolean
algoritma
  input(nmbr)
  value <- string(nmbr)
  nmbr <- integer(value)
  if nmbr < 2 then
    prima <- false
  else
    prima <- true
    lmt <- nmbr - 1
    for j <- 2 to lmt do
      rmndr <- nmbr mod j
      if rmndr == 0 then
        prima <- false
      endif
    endfor
  endif
  output(prima)
endprogram

metadata.modification_notes: The student systematically applies their vowel-based naming belief: 'value' (contains vowels a, u, e) is used for the string conversion, while all numeric variables use consonant-only names: 'nmbr' (number), 'lmt' (limit), 'j' (loop counter), and 'rmndr' (remainder). The student converts num to a string stored in 'value' because they believe vowel-containing names can only hold strings, then converts to int and stores in consonant-only 'nmbr' to perform numeric operations. This pattern demonstrates their belief that Python enforces type restrictions based on vowel presence in variable names. The code will cause a runtime TypeError when called with an integer argument since str() works but the unnecessary conversion reveals the flawed understanding.
